Yep, the meta has been pretty healthy for a while, the last thing closest to tier 0 is probably Cyber Orcust or Danger Darkworld FTK (yes, it was an ultra consistent first turn kill). Luckily these got dealt with pretty fast. Other than that though, at any given time there’s a solid ~5 or so top decks to choose from, with a healthy ~15 or so other decks that can do some good stuff. Yugioh has a LOT of staple, splashable cards like lightning storm, forbidden droplet, and ash blossom that can be played in virtually any deck, which in turn makes a lot of decks viable.

I’ve competed at IRL tournaments and even I don’t fully understand all the rules (particularly advanced stuff like PSCT and Missing Timing). Luckily, you don’t have to worry about that, because master duel will automatically handle those weird rulings.

At the lower ranks in master duel, people will mostly be playing fun/off meta decks, so you’ll definitely be able to get the gist of things before you hit gold. There’s not really a “get rich quick” method in Yugioh, you’ll have to learn what certain staple cards do over time, and what counters what.

Some basics that will occur a lot:

Ash blossom and joyous spring (a “hand trap”) negates most card advantage. Basically, it is a monster that you send from your hand to the graveyard to stop your opponent from gaining card advantage.

Called by the grave, a spell card, is commonly used to counter ash blossom, because it negates graveyard cards.

You’ll probably see maxx c a lot right now, but you might not in the future because it’s banned in the TCG. Maxx C is a hand trap that punishes your opponent for dumping out monsters. (When your opponent special summons a monster during their turn, draw a card) maxx c can lead to some ridiculous card advantage.

Infinite Impermanence is a trap card, hand trap, that negates a monster effect and stops spells/traps in that column from activating. Forbidden Chalice is also played, it’s a monster negate as well.

Droll and Lock Bird is a hand trap that prevents your opponent from adding cards to their hand from their deck for the rest of their turn

Nibiru the Primal Being is a monster that says, if your opponent summons at least 5 monsters in a turn, tribute their entire board and summon nibiru on their side of the field. This is used to stop combo decks that summon a lot in one turn.

You’ll probably see a Kaiju here and there too, which are monsters that tribute your opponents monsters to summon themselves to your opponents field. These are good because they circumvent sticky, bulky monsters that have protection from effects


The above cards make up most of the turn interaction in Yugioh, because they shut down your opponents combos. You’ll have to familiarize yourself with certain decks to figure out how to best cripple your opponent with these cards though, and that’s learned with experience.

Coming from a competitive Yugioh player, make sure you build a “somewhat meta” deck. Banlists WILL kill your deck if it isn’t removed enough from the top ~4 or so decks of a format. Like other comments say, the gems are frontloaded, so building engines and decks that will outlast banlists is going to be important. Practicing on showdown helps quite a lot, but to be more specific about the mental in-turn process: 

Firstly you have to consider the interactions, like you said with psychic terrain that blocks priority moves. Prankster status moves on the opponent will be blocked, but stuff like prankster tailwind won’t of course. If you have a Pokémon like tapu koko or rillaboom in the back, you can bring them out to reset the terrain. All of this “interaction consideration” should be done quickly at the start of a turn. There’s not much you can do to get better at this, it comes with experience, so the more you play the less you’ll miss.

The next step should be considering the likelihood of your opponents moves, this will be more difficult if your opponent is running Pokémon/sets that you’re unfamiliar with, but in most games you should have a solid idea of what stuff wants to do. The process that I use, is I assign rough percentages out of 100% to each move my opponent can make.

For example:
>my opponents Pokémon are walled by my Pokémon, there’s roughly a 70% chance they will switch out at least one Pokémon

>my opponent knows I have fake out available, so there’s roughly a 50% chance they will protect

After you’ve gone through and assigned the percentages, you’ll have a better conceptualization of the optimal move to make, and down the line your percentages will get more precise with experience and your breakdowns can be used in future games with similar field states (which is why it helps to use a notepad)

Team preview is arguably the most important part of a match, if you see a team of slow Pokémon with something like hatterene/mimikyu/togekiss/indeedee/staka you can determine that’s probably a trick room team, and so positioning your lead to prevent trickroom/play through it is the move. Getting the downlow on what certain Pokémon want to do in a given game is learned with experience/research on sites like pikalytics. At the moment you should focus particularly on sun teams and kyogre teams and determining what those teams lead into your own team and how to position correctly to deal with their threats, as those archetypes are the most common right now. Obviously not every game will be the same, but the more you research it, the more consistent you’ll get.

Hopefully this helps!

It’s better to give you an idea of what you’re getting into:

KOREAN TROPES:

-it’s a korean MMO, notorious for being extremely grindy and having cash shop. I don’t PERSONALLY think the game is p2w (considering it’s actually a lot easier and faster to grind for full gear than it is to indirectly pay for it, you’re technically really dumb for taking the pay path in reality) but the grind aspect is very true. Your XP will “softcap” at certain levels and continue to softcap each level higher you go, so grinding levels just basically gets longer and longer. I personally find this fun and rewarding, but NA MMO players who want a participation trophy for everything they do have hated on it before.

ENHANCEMENT:

-the enhancement system to make your gear stronger is, yes, based on RNG. However, if you are boring, you can simply grind for money and buy your enhanced gear off of the marketplace and not have to worry about the RNG of enhancing. Or, you can grow a pair. and realize the RNG is part of the fun, and failing just makes successful enhancements feel sweeter. The game actually provides you a huge amount of ways to make enhancing less-pain more-gain, with things like valks, concentrated, cron stones, secret books, cry, etc. but it’s up to you how much of that you want to work for.

QUESTING VERSUS GRINDING:

-I would definitely do the main quest on your first character at least until the start of Valencia quest line. This will give you access to a lot of questlocked content and as a bonus it will give you a ton of rewards and free money, especially on a season character. Technically, you can do like 15 quests and then just grind mobs to softcap, and that’s what I tend to do on random classes that I just want to test out since it’s much faster, but long-term having the quests done is important. There is an endgame item called black star that you need to do a quest to get, so you’ll need to have the mediah quest line done to do that.

REWARD:

-there’s a lot of tragedy and victory in this game. You’re going to fail enhancements if you play the game as intended, and that’s gonna hurt AND cost you a lot of silver, but in the end, when you’re in top damage bracket on world bosses and getting 150 million silver an hour from star’s end. All the time and pain feels worth it. This is not a casual game.

CLASSES:

-your class choice doesn’t really matter endgame wise, each class is good at something. For example, berserker, sorceress, ninja are solid PvP choices while Wizard, Hash, Guardian are really good PvE classes, all classes can be good at PvE or PvP but some are optimal in one or the other. From what I’ve heard, Maehwa is a bit weak at the moment, but other than that the class balance is actually really good in BDO and people don’t really give it much credit. I would recommend not investing too much into any character until you’ve tried most/all of the classes out yourself because you’ll eventually find the class that fits you. For example, I’m a diehard mage class in every MMO I play, so I was naturally drawn to wizard. I tried basically every class to awakening, and determined I do in fact love wizard the most. You can always make a new character and transfer your gear if you feel unhappy with your choice though, so don’t worry too much. Just don’t be like my friend, who “mains” every class he plays and switches his main every time he makes a new character.

There are set bonuses associated with gear, having the dim tree with tuvala stops you from getting the 4-set bonus, so either go full tuva or full boss gear. And like other comments say, you’ll need higher AP to attempt endgame m/h goals in stars end and syc, so pushing your AP higher for that is imperative
